analysis.one_liner: Bans future sales of military-style semiautomatic weapons and large magazines and expands background checks.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 5 cosponsors but never advanced past its committee referral in January 2019; it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFER Now Act would have banned the future manufacture, sale, and transfer of semiautomatic assault weapons and ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, while letting people who already owned them keep them. It would also have required a background check before a dealer could hand over any gun, extended federal gun bans to people convicted of misdemeanor stalking and to abusive dating partners, made gun trafficking a stand-alone crime, and imposed registration and background-check rules on gun shows. The bill never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to gun violence, especially in mass shootings with military-style rifles and high-capacity magazines; domestic violence victims, because the bill would extend federal gun prohibitions to misdemeanor stalkers and dating partners covered by restraining orders; and police, who would be notified when a prohibited person tries to buy a grandfathered assault weapon.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to gun violence and domestic abuse

how_it_helps.text: Closes a gap in the background check system so a licensed dealer cannot transfer a firearm to an unlicensed buyer before the background check is complete, rather than after a waiting period expires.

Prohibits the import, sale, manufacture, transfer, or possession of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition feeding devices, with exceptions for current lawful owners, police, and other specified holders.

Requires a background check through a licensed dealer before any private sale or transfer of a grandfathered semiautomatic assault weapon, and requires police to be notified when a prohibited person attempts to buy one.
Makes firearms trafficking a stand-alone criminal offense carrying up to 20 years in prison, aimed at people who buy guns intending to hand them to someone prohibited from owning one.

Adds misdemeanor stalking convictions to the list of disqualifying offenses and expands the definition of 'intimate partner' to include dating partners, extending existing domestic-violence gun prohibitions to abusers the current law misses.
Requires gun show operators to register with the Attorney General and requires a background check before any firearm transfer between unlicensed people at a gun show.
Bans bump-fire devices, trigger cranks, and any accessory designed to increase the firing rate of a semiautomatic rifle without converting it into a machine gun.

analysis.who_pays: Gun manufacturers whose best-selling product lines — AR-15 and AK-pattern rifles, pistols, and magazines over 10 rounds — would be newly banned from manufacture and sale; gun show operators facing registration, recordkeeping, and inspection requirements; and makers of rate-of-fire accessories, whose products would be banned outright.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and gun show operators

drawbacks.text: The ban is grandfathered: people who lawfully owned the weapons and magazines before enactment could keep them, so the millions already in circulation would remain with their owners indefinitely, with only a safe-storage requirement around prohibited persons.

The definition of 'semiautomatic assault weapon' is broad, reaching any semiautomatic rifle with a pistol grip, forward grip, folding stock, barrel shroud, or threaded barrel, and naming many common models; a good-faith objection is that this sweeps in ordinary hunting and sporting rifles rather than only military-style ones.

The buy-back program is voluntary: Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funds could pay people to surrender banned weapons and magazines, but no one would be required to turn them in, so the stock of existing weapons would shrink only slowly.
The bill exempts law enforcement officers, retired officers, nuclear facility security licensees, and others from the bans, so the restricted weapons remain available to those categories.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main public benefit — a smaller future supply of military-style rifles and high-capacity magazines and tighter checks on who can buy them — is real but delayed, because current owners keep everything they already have and buy-backs are voluntary. The main cost falls on a specific industry and on gun owners who would face new limits on future purchases and transfers. The breadth of the weapon definitions is the strongest design criticism; a narrower list, or a stronger mechanism for retiring existing weapons, would have addressed it without giving up the core protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and neither ever scheduled a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joyce Beatty introduced the SAFER Now Act on January 8, 2019, joined by Reps. Eleanor Holmes Norton, Betty McCollum, and Jahana Hayes as original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill ended with 5 cosponsors, all House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers and sellers of the named rifles, high-capacity magazines, and rate-of-fire accessories kept their market, since no new restrictions took effect; buyers also retained full access to these products. No restrictions were added for domestic abusers or stalkers beyond those already in law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and sellers kept their market

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited three original cosponsors.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no member of the other party did.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security

against.name: National Rifle Association and allied gun-rights groups
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed federal bans on semiautomatic rifles and high-capacity magazines during this period, helping keep such bills from reaching the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; on the record the bill was supported only by Democrats, with the sponsor and all 5 cosponsors House Democrats.

industries.note: The bill bans future manufacture, sale, and import of semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns on its named and feature-based lists, plus magazines over 10 rounds — the most commercially successful civilian firearm categories. Manufacturers keep selling to police and to exempt buyers, and nothing forces retirement of guns already sold, but their civilian growth market closes.

Dealers lose sales of newly banned weapons, but the bill makes them the mandatory channel for background checks on private transfers of grandfathered assault weapons and all gun-show transfers, a fee-based role only they can perform.

Operators would have to register with the Attorney General, submit fingerprints and fees, verify and log every vendor, and open their records to warrantless inspections — a compliance burden designed to stop unlicensed sales at shows.
Bump-fire devices, trigger cranks, and any part designed to accelerate a semiautomatic rifle's rate of fire would be banned from manufacture, sale, and possession, eliminating that product line.
